content: The most common adverse effects of sulfamethoxazole include gastrointestinal disturbances such as nausea, vomiting, and anorexia, as well as allergic skin reactions like rash and urticaria. Although rare, fatalities have been reported due to severe reactions associated with sulfonamide administration. These severe reactions include Stevens-Johnson syndrome, toxic epidermal necrolysis, fulminant hepatic necrosis, agranulocytosis, aplastic anemia, and other blood dyscrasias. Hematologic effects may include agranulocytosis, aplastic anemia, thrombocytopenia, leukopenia, neutropenia, hemolytic anemia, megaloblastic anemia, hypoprothrombinemia, methemoglobinemia, and eosinophilia. Allergic reactions can manifest as Stevens-Johnson syndrome, toxic epidermal necrolysis, anaphylaxis, allergic myocarditis, erythema multiforme, exfoliative dermatitis, angioedema, drug fever, chills, Henoch-Schönlein purpura, serum sickness-like syndrome, generalized allergic reactions, generalized skin eruptions, photosensitivity, conjunctival and scleral injection, pruritus, urticaria, and rash. Additionally, periarteritis nodosa and systemic lupus erythematosus have been reported. Gastrointestinal effects include hepatitis (including cholestatic jaundice and hepatic necrosis), elevated serum transaminase and bilirubin levels, pseudomembranous enterocolitis, pancreatitis, stomatitis, glossitis, nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain, diarrhea, and anorexia. Genitourinary effects may involve renal failure, interstitial nephritis, elevated BUN and serum creatinine levels, toxic nephrosis with oliguria and anuria, crystalluria, and nephrotoxicity, particularly in association with cyclosporine. Metabolic and nutritional effects include hyperkalemia and hyponatremia. Neurologic effects may present as aseptic meningitis, seizures, peripheral neuritis, ataxia, vertigo, tinnitus, and headache. Psychiatric effects include hallucinations, depression, apathy, and nervousness. Endocrine effects are related to the chemical similarities of sulfonamides to certain goitrogens, diuretics (e.g., acetazolamide and thiazides), and oral hypoglycemic agents. Cross-sensitivity with these agents may occur. Rarely, diuresis and hypoglycemia have been observed in patients receiving sulfonamides. Musculoskeletal effects include arthralgia and myalgia. Isolated cases of rhabdomyolysis have been reported, primarily in AIDS patients treated with Bactrim. Respiratory effects may include cough, shortness of breath, and pulmonary infiltrates. Miscellaneous effects include weakness, fatigue, and insomnia. Postmarketing experience has identified additional adverse reactions, including thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura, idiopathic thrombocytopenic purpura, and QT prolongation, which can result in ventricular tachycardia and torsades de pointes. These reactions were reported voluntarily and from a population of uncertain size, making it difficult to reliably estimate their frequency or establish a causal relationship to drug exposure.
